title: Celebrity deaths in 2026: Remembering the famous people we lost this year
summary: Stars we've lost this year include Dolly Parton, Eva Marie Saint, Patrick Stewart, Hayden Panettiere, James Van Der Beek, and Gloria Steinem.
content: Andy Taylor. Dave Hogan/Hulton Archive/Getty Images Actors James Van Der Beek, Hayden Panettiere, Robert Duvall, Chuck Norris, Patrick Stewart, and Eva Marie Saint died in 2026. So did musicians Dolly Parton and Duncan Sheik. Civil rights leader Rev. Jesse Jackson, activist Gloria Steinem, and NFL Hall of Famer Mike Ditka also died this year. Below, we look back at the celebrities we lost in 2026, listed in alphabetical order. Scott Adams, 68 Scott Adams. Michael Macor/Getty Images Scott Adams worked at a telephone company in the 1980s. The experience inspired his beloved comic strip, "Dilbert." By the end of the decade, the character and his satirical office humor began appearing in comic strips. At its peak, "Dilbert" was syndicated in over 2,000 newspapers. A cartoon series debuted in 1999, running for two seasons. Adams gained notoriety when he began writing blog posts praising Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run. In 2023, "Dilbert" was pulled from newspapers across the US following racist comments made by Adams. Adams died on January 13 from metastatic prostate cancer . Brad Arnold, 47 Brad Arnold. Scott Gries/ImageDirect/Getty Images The lead singer of 3 Doors Down, Brad Arnold launched the group into fame with the 2000 rock anthem "Kryptonite," which peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 that year. The success led to other hits like "Loser," "Here Without You," and "When I'm Gone." Arnold's vocal range and lyrics focused on love and love lost, which fueled the group to stardom. Arnold died on February 7 from a type of kidney cancer. Afrika Bambaataa, 68 Afrika Bambaataa. Paul Natkin/WireImage/Getty A hip-hop pioneer during the 1970s and 1980s, Lance Taylor, known professionally as Afrika Bambaataa, first gained attention as a DJ in the Bronx. He signed with Tommy Boy Records in 1981 and released landmark songs like "Jazzy Sensation" and "Planet Rock." He would go on to influence the likes of Queen Latifah and A Tribe Called Quest throughout his career. Bambaataa founded the hip-hop awareness group, Universal Zulu Nation, in the 1970s to steer kids away from gang life. Bambaataa stepped down as the head of the organization in 2016 after accusations of sexual abuse . Bambaataa denied all claims. He died on April 9 due to prostate cancer . Rob Bass, 59 Rob Bass. Al Pereira/Michael Osche Archives/Getty Images One of the icons responsible for bringing hip-hop to the mainstream, Rob Bass crafted the iconic track "It Takes Two" alongside DJ E-Z Rock. The track, released in 1988, reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot Dance/Club Songs chart and later went certified platinum. In 1989, it was voted the greatest single of all time by Spin magazine. Bass died on May 22 following cancer . Nicholas Brendon, 54 Nicholas Brendon. Getty Images Nicholas Brendon was a television actor, best known for playing Xander Harris in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer." He also starred in "Criminal Minds" and "Kitchen Confidential." Brendon died in his sleep on March 20 due to natural causes, according to his family's statement. In 2023, Brendon suffered a heart attack and was diagnosed with a congenital heart defect. He also had cauda equina syndrome, which led to several spinal surgeries. "While it's no secret that Nicholas had struggles in the past, he was on medications and treatment to manage his diagnosis, and he was optimistic about the future at the time of his passing," the statement to The Hollywood Reporter read. "Our family asks for privacy during this time as we grieve his loss and celebrate the life of a man who lived with intensity, imagination, and heart." Peabo Bryson, 75 Peabo Bryson. ABC Photo Archives/Getty Images Two-time Grammy winner Peabo Bryson is best known for his classic love ballads. Bryson began releasing music in the late 1970s, but one of his first major hits was opposite Roberta Flack on the 1983 duet, "Tonight, I Celebrate My Love." He continued hit-making a year later with the smash "If Ever You're in My Arms Again," and in 1991, he topped the R&B charts with "Can You Stop the Rain." Bryson found global stardom with his renditions of two Disney classics. In 1991, he released the pop version of "Beauty and the Beast," alongside Céline Dion, and a year later, he duetted with Regina Belle on "A Whole New World" from the 1992 release of "Aladdin." Bryson died on June 2. No cause was given. James Burrows, 85 James Burrows. Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images An 11-time Emmy winner and co-creator of "Cheers," director James Burrows helped shape modern TV comedy through his work on iconic sitcoms including "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "Frasier." Known for his comedic timing and elaborate blocking, Burrows got his start directing episodes of "The Mary Tyler Moore Show." Throughout his career, he directed episodes of "Frasier" (winning an Emmy for the pilot episode), "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "The Big Bang Theory." He directed over 50 pilot episodes. Burrows died on June 19. No cause was given. Kyle Busch, 41 Kyle Busch. Sean Gardner/Getty Images Two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion Busch was considered one of the greatest racers of all time. Busch was hospitalized on May 21, before two upcoming races. Hours later, he was pronounced dead. Busch died from severe pneumonia that progressed into sepsis. Robert Carradine, 71 Robert Carradine. Bobby Bank/WireImage/Getty Robert Carradine was best known for his roles as Lizzie McGuire's dad and as the iconic geek Lewis Skolnick in the 1980s franchise "Revenge of the Nerds." As a member of Hollywood's famed Carradine family, Robert was destined for an onscreen career. He received one of his first screen credits starring in his brother David Carradine's popular 1970s TV series "Kung Fu" and went on to land roles in everything from Samuel Fuller's World War II classic "The Big Red One" to the "Lizzie McGuire" series. Carradine's family shared statements with Deadline that emphasized being open about his struggles with mental illness. "We are bereft at the loss of this beautiful soul and want to acknowledge Bobby's valiant struggle against his nearly two-decade battle with Bipolar Disorder," Carradine's family said. "We hope his journey can shine a light and encourage addressing the stigma that attaches to mental illness." Carradine died by suicide on February 23. If you or someone you know is experiencing depression or has had thoughts of harming themself or taking their own life, get help. In the US, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline . Help is also available through the Crisis Text Line — just text "HOME" to 741741. The International Association for Suicide Prevention offers resources for those outside the US. Bud Cort, 77 Bud Cort. CBS Photo Archive/CBS via Getty Images Most famous for his role as Harold in the 1971 cult-classic "Harold and Maude," Bud Cort became the epitome of 1970s counterculture thanks to his baby-faced looks, wit, and sophisticated persona. The dark comedy starred Cort as Harold, a man in his 20s who is obsessed with suicide until he meets 79-year-old eccentric Maude (Ruth Gordon). Before that, Cort scored bit parts in Robert Altman's "M*A*S*H*" (1970) and "Brewster McCloud" (1970). After "Harold and Maude," Cort worked steadily for the rest of his life, occasionally showing up in hit movies like Michael Mann's "Heat" (1995) and Wes Anderson's "The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou" (2004). Cort died on February 11 following a long illness . Tim Curry, 80 Tim Curry. Evening Standard/Hulton Archive/Getty Images Curry is best known for playing Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the cult-classic musical "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," after originating the role in the original stage production. Over six decades, Curry carved out a niche playing outlandish villains like Rooster Hannigan in the 1982 film "Annie" and Pennywise in the 1990 miniseries "It." Other notable roles include Wadsworth the Butler in "Clue" (1985) and Mr. Hector in "Home Alone 2: Escape from New York." Curry suffered a major stroke in 2012, which required brain surgery. He said in 2025 that he was "still recovering." Curry died at his Los Angeles home on August 26. No cause was given. Eric Dane, 53 Eric Dane Pief Weyman/NBC via Getty Images Long before becoming one of TV's most recognizable heartthrobs, Eric Dane was building his career with guest roles on series like "Saved by the Bell" and "Married… with Children." He later gained wider attention with appearances on "Charmed" before landing his breakout role as Dr. Mark "McSteamy" Sloan on "Grey's Anatomy." He most recently starred in HBO's "Euphoria," where he played Cal Jacobs, the father of Jacob Elordi's character, Nate Jacobs. Dane has two children with his wife, Rebecca Gayheart. In April 2025, the actor said that he was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis , or ALS. Dane died on February 19 at age 53, his publicist confirmed in a statement to Business Insider. "He spent his final days surrounded by dear friends, his devoted wife, and his two beautiful daughters, Billie and Georgia, who were the center of his world," his publicist said. Clive Davis, 94 Clive Davis. Roy Rochlin/Getty Images A legend in the music world, Davis was responsible for elevating pop music to unthinkable heights by discovering talents like Aretha Franklin, Barry Manilow, Bruce Springsteen, Billy Joel, Whitney Houston, and Alicia Keys, to name a few. Over his 50-year career, along with being an executive behind millions of album sales, he also won five Grammys, including two for Album of the Year ("The Bodyguard" soundtrack and "Supernatural" by Santana). Davis died on June 22. No cause was given. Mike Ditka, 86 Chicago Bears head coach Mike Ditka gets carried off the field after they defeated the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XX on January 26, 1986. Focus on Sport/Getty Images Mike Ditka was the first tight end ever inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. As a coach for the Chicago Bears, he led the team to its only Super Bowl win to date in 1986. Ditka's success turned him into a celebrity who showed up in commercials, TV shows, and movies in cameo roles. One of his most famous was starring opposite Will Ferrell in the 2005 comedy "Kicking and Screaming." His persona became the long-running "Saturday Night Live" sketch called "Bill Swerski's Superfans," in which cast members dressed up as Ditka and spoke about their love for "Da Bears." Ditka died on October 9; no cause was given. Robert Duvall, 95 Robert Duvall. Jack Mitchell/Getty Images Robert Duvall starred in a plethora of timeless classics, including "The Godfather," "The Godfather Part II," "Apocalypse Now," "THX 1138," "The Natural," "Days of Thunder," and "The Apostle." Duvall will be best remembered for starring in three of director Francis Ford Coppola's iconic films: playing Tom Hagen in the first two "Godfather" movies and Lieutenant Colonel Bill Kilgore in "Apocalypse Now," in which he delivers one of the most memorable lines in movie history: "I love the smell of napalm in the morning." Duvall was lauded for his acting talent, from not saying a word while playing Boo Radley in his first big screen role in the 1962 classic "To Kill a Mockingbird" to his portrayal of a country singer dealing with alcoholism in 1983's "Tender Mercies," which earned him an Oscar. He died on his ranch in Virginia on February 15. No cause was given. Brenda Fricker, 81 Brenda Fricker in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York." 20th Century Fox This Irish actress was a fixture on the stage and screen for six decades. But she's most known for showing up in the "Home Alone" sequel. As The Pigeon Lady in 1992's "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Fricker has become a fixture for families during the holiday season for decades (and in 2020 became the subject of a popular meme ). But Fricker's acting talents go beyond playing a spooky wanderer of Central Park. In 1990, she became the first Irish actress to win an Academy Award, as she was given the best supporting actress Oscar that year for her performance in "My Left Foot." Fricker died on July 16; no cause was given. Mark Fuhrman, 74 Mark Fuhrman. Jim Smeal/Ron Galella Collection/Getty Images Fuhrman cemented his place in popular culture as one of the lead LAPD detectives on the 1995 murder case of O.J. Simpson's ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman. Fuhrman found the famed bloody glove on the Simpson estate, and during the trial, he gained infamy when Simpson's defense team used his past racist language to discredit him as a witness. Fuhrman retired from the LAPD after the Simpson trial and moved to Idaho, where he wrote true crime books. Fuhrman died on May 12 of throat cancer . Valentino Garavani, 93 Valentino Garavani. Stephane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty Images For over six decades, one name has been synonymous with women's high fashion: Valentino. The Italian designer launched his fashion business in Rome in 1960 and never looked back. Soon, every star wanted to be seen in his creations. They've been worn by icons like Elizabeth Taylor, Joan Collins, Jackie Kennedy, Princess Diana, Sharon Stone, and more. Though Garavani retired from designing in 2008, his label is still a red carpet staple, as is his famous shade of bright red dubbed "Valentino Red." Garavani died on January 19 . No cause was given. Donald Gibb, 71 Donald Gibb. 20th Century Fox No one defined a bully for a generation more than Gibb's hulking fraternity character Ogre in the "Revenge of the Nerds" movies of the 1980s. Since the original raunchy comedy was released in 1984, Gibb's intimidating size and loud yells of "NERDS!" have become as memorable as the pocket protectors worn by the movie's geeks. Gibb went on to star opposite Jean-Claude Van Damme in his classic 1988 action movie "Bloodsport." He also landed guest star roles through his career on shows like "Quantum Leap," "Magnum P.I.," "MacGyver," "Night Court," and "Cheers." Gibb died on May 12 following health complications . Chad Gilbert, 45 Chad Gilbert. Andrew Benge/Redferns/Getty Gilbert was the guitarist and backing vocalist for the punk band New Found Glory. The band's hit albums include 2002's "Sticks And Stones" and 2004's "Catalyst." Both showed up in the top 10 on the Billboard 200 chart. Gilbert died on September 20; no cause was given, but Gilbert told People in April he was battling stage 4 adrenal cancer. Glen Hansard, 56 Glen Hansard. Frank Hoensch/Redferns/Getty Irish singer-songwriter Hansard was the frontman of the rock band The Frames and one-half of the band The Swell Season. But he was perhaps best known for writing and starring in the hit 2007 indie film "Once," in which he and his Swell Season bandmate Markéta Irglová play two struggling musicians who fall in love. The duo won an Oscar for best original song for the film's standout track, " Falling Slowly. " Hansard also embarked on a solo career; his 2015 album, "Didn't He Ramble," was nominated for a Grammy for best folk album. Hansard died on July 29 in a motorcycle crash in Dublin. Dennis Haskins, 75 Dennis Haskins. NBC/Getty Images For those who grew up in the '90s, Dennis Haskins was your favorite high school principal, Mr. Belding. Starring in the hit TV series "Saved By The Bell," Haskins' Belding character traveled the halls trying to be a step ahead of the hijinks inflicted by Zack Morris (Mark-Paul Gosselaar) and his friends. But unlike many school principals in pop culture who were mean and seemed to hate kids, Haskins played his authority role with a playful, good-natured style. He was on the show's full four-season run from 1989 to 1993, and also starred in the spin-off, "Saved By The Bell: The New Class," from 1993 to 2000. Haskins' other credits include "The Bold and the Beautiful," "Mad Men," "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia," and "New Girl." Haskins died on September 27; no cause was given. Anthony Head, 72 Anthony Head. James Quinton/WireImage/Getty Rising up through the UK stage scene in the 1980s, Head found fame when he was cast as Rupert Giles, who became a father figure to Sarah Michelle Gellar's Buffy Summers in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer." Most recently, he played the bitter former owner of AFC Richmond on "Ted Lasso." Head's death was announced by his family on June 5. They stated the cause was "complications due to pneumonia." David Hockney, 88 David Hockney at home in Los Angeles in 1987. Anthony Barboza/Getty Images British painter David Hockney was renowned for his striking portraits and figurative pop art. Many of his best-known paintings, including 1966's "The Splash" and 1972's "Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)," were inspired by the bright colors and sun-dappled pools of Los Angeles. Hockney moved to Los Angeles in the late '60s, and his work became synonymous with the warmth and leisure of Southern California. He was also one of the few popular artists at the time to depict openly gay scenes, and Hockney was outspoken about anti-gay censorship. Throughout his career, Hockney split time between California, England, and France. He died at his home in London on June 12 at age 88, his publicist confirmed to The New York Times . No cause of death was given. Jesse Jackson, 84 Rev. Jesse Jackson speaks at Operation PUSH in Chicago, Illinois in December 1989. Raymond Boyd/Getty Images The Rev. Jesse Jackson was a leader of the Civil Rights Movement, a minister, and an activist icon who twice ran for president. Born on October 8, 1941, in Greenville, South Carolina, Jackson experienced Jim Crow segregation on public buses and at school firsthand. It would shape the rest of his life. His fight for civil rights began in the 1960s, when he helped organize protests and demonstrations across the US and worked closely alongside civil rights icon Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. His decadeslong career as a leading civil rights activist included support for modern national movements, such as the push for voting rights, the fight against racism, and a higher minimum wage. Jackson ran for president twice, both times as a democrat. He placed third for the party's nomination in 1984 and second in 1988. This marked the most successful presidential runs of any Black candidate prior to Barack Obama. Jackson announced in 2017 that he'd been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. In November 2025, Jackson was treated in a Chicago hospital after complications from progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), a rare neurodegenerative condition. Jackson died on February 17. Stacy Keach, 85 Stacy Keach. CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images Keach brought intensity and charisma to every role he played on stage, film, and TV. He was a major player in Off-Broadway and Broadway productions of Shakespearean works in the late 1960s, earning him awards and a Tony nomination. He would go on to gain steady work on TV and movies the rest of his career. He was perhaps best known for playing private eye Mike Hammer in the 1980s TV series "Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer," and won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in the 1988 miniseries "Hemingway." Later in his career, he developed a knack for playing the villain in movies like "American History X" (1998) and "Nebraska" (2013). Keach died on November 10 after heart failure complicated by heart disease. Walter Koenig, 90 Walter Koenig as Pavel Chekov in season 2 of "Star Trek." CBS/Getty Images As the boyish Russian crewman Pavel Chekov on "Star Trek," Walter Koenig left an indelible mark in the minds of sci-fi fans for generations as one of the key crew members of Captain Kirk's ship, the USS Enterprise. First appearing in the show's second season, Koenig played Chekov in 36 of the 50 episodes that aired in 1967-68 and 1968-69. He also starred in the first seven releases of the movie franchise, from 1979 through 1991. Koenig died on October 25 of natural causes . Yayoi Kusama, 97 Yayoi Kusama presented an "Infinity Room" installation in Paris. Alain Nogues/Sygma/Sygma via Getty Images Kusama was a famed Japanese pop artist who often used polka-dot motifs in her work, initially rising to prominence in Japan in the 1950s. In 1959, Kusama presented her first solo exhibition in New York: a collection of abstract paintings that an ARTnews review praised as "strong, advanced in concept and realized." Kusama later branched into sculptures, performances, and immersive installations. She continued to expand her influence and relevance into the social media era, when her mirrored "Infinity Room" installations became Instagram-friendly attractions that inspired many copycats . Kusama died on August 14 in Tokyo. She was 97. Bob Mackie, 87 Bob Mackie. Mel Melcon/Getty Images As one of Hollywood's most renowned costume designers, Bob Mackie's eye set the style for decades. Known as the Sultan of Sequins, the Rajah of Rhinestones, or the Guru of Glitter, a signature of Mackie's work was its use of sparkle, which made everyone from Cher to Elton John to Dolly Parton to Sabrina Carpenter shine on stage. He also was the costume designer on "The Carol Burnett Show" for all eleven seasons through the 1970s. He won nine Emmys, a Tony Award, and was nominated for three Academy Awards for his work. Mackie died on September 14; no cause was given. RJ Mitte, 34 RJ Mitte. Rodin Eckenroth/FilmMagic/Getty Mitte was best known for playing the son of Bryan Cranston's Walter White in the hit series "Breaking Bad." Mitte, who was diagnosed with cerebral palsy when he was 3 years old, became a disability rights activist after finding fame with "Breaking Bad." His other credits include the 2021 movie "Triumph," in which he played a high school student with cerebral palsy who tries out for the wrestling team. He also starred in the 2024 thriller "Love Me Dead" opposite Dove Cameron. Mitte died by suicide on October 12. Patrick Muldoon, 57 Patrick Muldoon. Mitchell Haaseth/NBC/Getty In the 1990s, you couldn't escape the piercing eyes of Patrick Muldoon. He played Austin Reed on "Days of Our Lives" for most of the decade, and when he wasn't on the soap, he was over on "Melrose Place" playing the villain role of Richard Hart. If being on two iconic shows wasn't enough, he also showed up on "Saved by the Bell" and had a role in the cult classic movie "Starship Troopers." Muldoon died on April 19 after a heart attack . Sam Neill, 78 Sam Neill. Nick Haddow/Penske Media/Getty Images With a career spanning more than five decades and including countless memorable performances in movies and television, Sam Neill was one of the most versatile actors of his generation, The New Zealand actor starred opposite Nicole Kidman in the 1989 thriller "Dead Calm," played the loyal first officer opposite Sean Connery in 1990's "The Hunt for Red October," played the lead in John Carpenter's 1994 horror "In the Mouth of Madness," and most recently starred in the hit series "Peaky Blinders." But Neill is best known for playing the brave and all-dinosaur-knowing Dr. Alan Grant in the "Jurassic Park" franchise. Neill died on July 13; no cause was given. Neill was battling a rare and aggressive form of blood cancer, but was cancer-free at the time of his death, according to a post on his Instagram account announcing his passing . Tom Noonan, 74 Tom Noonan. Mike Albans/New York Daily News Archive/Getty Images Standing at a towering 6' 5", Tom Noonan was born to play the bad guy. And he did just that, starring as the villain in movies like "Manhunter," "RoboCop 2," and "Last Action Hero." But this actor had more to show off. He showcased his comedy chops as Rodney Dangerfield's degenerate gambling friend in the 1983 comedy "Easy Money," and set up the heist for Robert De Niro in Michael Mann's 1995 classic "Heat." His knack for storytelling also translated behind the camera. Noonan wrote, directed, and starred in the drama "What Happened Was," which won the grand prize at the 1994 Sundance Film Festival. Noonan died on February 14; no cause was given. Chuck Norris, 86 Chuck Norris. Frederic Meylan/Getty Few action stars have Chuck Norris' credentials. Before he ever stepped in front of a camera, he was a martial arts champion and a black belt in Karate, judo, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, Taekwondo, and Tang Soo Do. His talents would become known the world over in 1972, when he faced off against Bruce Lee in "The Way of the Dragon." Through the 1980s, Norris became one of the biggest action stars in the world thanks to movies like "A Force of One," "The Octagon," and the "Delta Force" and "Missing in Action" franchises. In the 1990s, he took over the small screen, playing the lead in the "Walker, Texas Ranger" TV show, which aired in over 100 countries during its run from 1993 to 2001. Norris was hospitalized on March 19 in Hawaii and died the following day, according to his family . No cause was given. Catherine O'Hara, 71 Catherine O'Hara at the 2024 Oscars. Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images O'Hara, who was best known for her roles in "Beetlejuice" and "Home Alone," got her start in the Canadian comedy scene, appearing in the now-legendary cast of "SCTV." It would mark the beginning of a fruitful partnership with fellow actor Eugene Levy, who became her frequent costar and collaborator in memorable appearances in Christopher Guest films like "A Mighty Wind" and "Best in Show" and television series like "Schitt's Creek," which earned her an Emmy Award for outstanding lead actress in 2020. O'Hara's representative confirmed her death to Business Insider on January 30. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health confirmed in a death certificate viewed by People that O'Hara died of a pulmonary embolism, with rectal cancer listed as an underlying cause. Hayden Panettiere, 36 Hayden Panettiere. Roy Rochlin/FilmMagic/Getty Panettiere began acting as a child, landing one of her earliest major roles as Sarah Roberts on the ABC soap opera "One Life to Live," on which she appeared from 1994 to 1997. As her career progressed, she became best known for portraying Claire Bennet on "Heroes" and Juliette Barnes on "Nashville." Over the years, Panettiere had spoken openly about her struggles with alcoholism and postpartum depression. She detailed those experiences in her memoir, "This Is Me: A Reckoning," which was released in May. Panettiere died on August 16. A final autopsy report by the Greenville County Coroner's Office ruled her death an accident caused by the toxic effects of fentanyl and other drugs. Dolly Parton, 80 Dolly Parton poses for a portrait session in 1978. Harry Langdon/Getty Images Parton released her debut album, "Hello, I'm Dolly," in 1967 and went on to pen country hits like "I Will Always Love You" and "Jolene," both of which were released as singles in 1974. In addition to her music, Parton was beloved for her flamboyant style and her philanthropy . She founded the Dollywood Foundation in 1988, a charitable organization focused on education and community initiatives in her home state of Tennessee. She continued to fund scholarship programs and donate to hospitals, public health initiatives, and disaster relief programs throughout her life. Parton is known as the best-selling female country music artist of all time. She was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1999, the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2001, and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022. Parton's 49th and final solo studio album, "Rockstar," was released in 2023. The tracklist included both original material and covers of classic rock songs, featuring an array of guests like Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr, Sting, Joan Jett, and Parton's goddaughter, Miley Cyrus. News broke on August 25 that Parton died following unspecified health issues . She was 80. Vincent Pastore, 80 Vincent Pastore. Lawrence Lucier/FilmMagic/Getty This character actor found fame appearing in a string of mob movies in the 1990s, like "Goodfellas," "Carlito's Way," and "Men of Respect." But Pastore truly became a star when he was cast in the hit HBO series "The Sopranos." As Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero, Pastore was part of the main cast for the first two seasons of the show, playing Tony Soprano's mob enforcer-turned-FBI informant. Bonpensiero's shocking death was one of the most famous in the show's history and proved that no one was safe from getting whacked. Pastore died on August 1. No cause was given. Valerie Perrine, 82 Valerie Perrine. Stanley Bielecki Movie Collection/Getty Images Perrine found herself cast alongside the biggest stars of the 1970s. She played the love interest opposite Jeff Bridges in 1973's "The Last American Hero" and Robert Redford in 1979's "The Electric Horseman." She earned an Oscar nomination for starring alongside Dustin Hoffman in 1974's "Lenny." For most, she'll be remembered best for sharing the screen with Gene Hackman as the secretary to his evil Lex Luthor in 1978's "Superman." She also starred in the sequel. As Ms. Teschmacher, her loyalty to Luthor is questioned when she rescues Superman (Christopher Reeve) after he's chained with Kryptonite . Perrine died in her home in Beverly Hills on March 23. She was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2015 . Richard Riehle, 78 Richard Riehle. Renard Garr/FilmMagic/Getty A prolific character actor, Riehle has over 400 screen credits, appearing in everything from "Casino" to "Bridesmaids" over his career. He's best known for playing the worker in "Office Space" who, after being laid off, wins a large payout from a lawsuit after a suicide attempt. Other credits include "The Fugitive," "Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas," and "Transformers: Age of Extinction." Riehle died on October 15; no cause was given. Sonny Rollins, 95 Sonny Rollins. Jack Vartoogian/Getty Images One of the most influential jazz musicians in history, Rollins recorded more than 60 albums over his seven-decade career. His live album, "A Night at the Village Vanguard," is considered one of the greatest jazz albums ever made. Rollins died on May 25; no cause was given. Eva Marie Saint, 102 Eva Marie Saint. Getty Images An Oscar and Emmy winner, Eva Marie Saint appeared in classic movies in Hollywood history. She made her film debut starring opposite Marlon Brando in Elia Kazan's 1954 classic "On the Waterfront," which won her the Oscar for best supporting actress. In 1959, she heated up the screen with Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock's defining thriller "North by Northwest." In 1990, she won an Emmy for her work in the miniseries "People Like Us." Saint died on October 6 of natural causes . Susan Saint James, 80 Susan Saint James. Bob Coburn /American Broadcasting Companies/Getty Images Saint James was a fixture in television from the late 1960s through the 1980s, starring in "The Name of the Game," "McMillan & Wife," and "Kate & Allie." She was Emmy-nominated eight times and won an Emmy for lead actress in 1985 for "Kate & Allie." Saint James' movie credits include "Outlaw Blues" (1977), "Love at First Bite" (1979), and "How to Beat the High Cost of Living (1980). Saint James died on October 26 after being diagnosed with pancreatic cancer . Neil Sedaka, 86 Neil Sedaka. Bettmann Archive/Getty Sedaka is responsible for some of the biggest pop songs of the 1960s and 1970s. The Brooklyn native wrote over 500 songs, including classic hits like "Laughter in the Rain," "Breaking Up Is Hard to Do," "Bad Blood" and the Captain & Tennille song, "Love Will Keep Us Together." Sedaka died on February 27; no cause was given. Gene Shalit, 100 Gene Shalit. NBC/Getty Before there was Rotten Tomatoes or even Siskel & Ebert, movie lovers got their recommendations from Gene Shalit. The iconic movie critic could be seen sporting his signature look of glasses, bushy hair, and big mustache as a staple on the "Today" show from 1973 to 2010. If he wasn't interviewing the biggest movie stars, he was reviewing movies with incredible puns ("'Ishtar' is Ish-terrible.") His larger-than-life presence left a mark on pop culture: he was parodied as a Muppet and on countless episodes of "SCTV" and "Saturday Night Live." Shalit died on June 12; no cause was given. Duncan Sheik, 56 Duncan Sheik. J. Vespa/WireImage/Getty Sheik found success in the late 1990s with his hit song " Barely Breathing. " He later pivoted from alt-rock to a career on Broadway, composing the music for the Tony-winning musical "Spring Awakening." His other stage credits include "American Psycho" (2013) and "The Secret Life of Bees" (2019). Sheik died on September 17 after a cardiac arrest . Kiki Shepard, 74 Kiki Shepard. Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images In her 15-year tenure as a co-host on "Showtime at the Apollo," Kiki Shepard was considered royalty at Harlem's famed Apollo Theater. Known in the building as "Apollo Queen of Fashion" thanks to her dazzling outfits, Shepherd was a fixture on the show from 1987 to 2002. Throughout her career, Shepard also appeared on TV shows like "Baywatch," "A Different World," "NYPD Blue," and "Grey's Anatomy." Shepard died on March 16 after suffering a heart attack . Tom Skerritt, 93 Tom Skerritt. Will Hart/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal/Getty A beloved actor in Hollywood for over six decades, Tom Skerritt appeared in some legendary movies and television. Robert Altman gave Skerritt his big break when he cast him as the womanizing and sarcastic surgeon Captain "Duke" Forrest in the classic 1970 movie "M*A*S*H." Skerritt followed it up with a string of hits, including Altman's "Thieves Like Us" (1974), "The Turning Point" (1977), and a hilarious cameo in Cheech & Chong's classic debut movie "Up in Smoke" (1978). Then, Skerritt went sci-fi when Ridley Scott cast him as Captain Arthur Dallas in 1979's "Alien." Skerritt also scored a memorable role as Tom Cruise's flight instructor "Viper" in 1986's "Top Gun." On the small screen, Skerritt earned an Emmy for playing Sheriff Jimmy Brock on the hit series "Picket Fences," which ran from 1992 to 1996. Skerritt died on October 21 of natural causes . Gloria Steinem, 92 Gloria Steinem. Barbara Alper/Getty Images An icon in the women's liberation movement of the 1970s, Steinem dedicated most of her life to fighting sexism. Starting her career as a journalist, she became a columnist for the newly founded New York Magazine in 1968. She cofounded Ms. magazine in 1971, which focused on women's issues. She also helped launch the Women's Action Alliance, which focused on tackling sexism. Steinem was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013. Steinem died on September 2, according to a post on her social media . No cause was given. Patrick Stewart, 86 Patrick Stewart. Paul Harris/Getty Images In a career spanning over 60 years on stage and screen, Stewart is responsible for some of the most memorable characters in the biggest franchises. After getting his start with the Royal Shakespeare Company in the late 1960s, he found acclaim on the stage, performing Shakespearean classics like "Antony and Cleopatra" and "Hamlet," both of which earned him Laurence Olivier Awards. Hollywood soon came calling, leading him to star in epics like "Excalibur" (1981) and David Lynch's "Dune" (1984). But he would get his big break in 1987 when he was cast as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation." Fans quickly gravitated to this new captain of the USS Enterprise, and the show ran until 1994. He also reprised the Picard role in four movies in the franchise: "Star Trek Generations" (1994), "Star Trek: First Contact" (1996), "Star Trek: Insurrection" (1998), and "Star Trek: Nemesis" (2002), as well as in the TV series "Star Trek: Picard" (2020-2023). In 2000, he joined the comic-book world when he was cast as mutant Professor Charles Xavier, founder of the X-Men in the Marvel Comics. Stewart portrayed Xavier in several more "X-Men" films, and will reprise the role in the forthcoming MCU film "Avengers: Doomsday," out this December. Stewart died on October 28 after suffering from Alzheimer's and Lewy Body Dementia . Béla Tarr, 70 Béla Tarr. Sean Gallup/Getty Hungarian filmmaker Béla Tarr became a legend in the arthouse world for his unflinching work featuring several-minute-long takes. With movies like "Family Nest" (1979) and "The Turin Horse" (2011), Tarr showcased his slow cinema style while focusing on marginalized characters living bleak lives. Tarr pushed the envelope with his style when he made "Sátántangó" in 1994, which had a run time of 450 minutes. His work influenced several arthouse filmmakers, including Jim Jarmusch and Gus Van Sant's "Death Trilogy" ("Gerry," "Elephant," and "Last Days"). Tarr died on January 6 following a battle with a " long and serious illness ." Andy Taylor, 65 Andy Taylor. Virginia Turbett/Getty Images Andy Taylor was the guitarist who helped define the sound of the British band Duran Duran, including on hits like "A View to a Kill" and "Hungry Like the Wolf." Taylor joined Duran Duran in April 1980 after answering the band's ad for a "live-wire guitarist" in a music magazine. The Newcastle native impressed the other band members at an audition and moved to Birmingham after getting the job. Taylor left Duran Duran in 1986 to pursue a solo career. He also collaborated with artists including Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle. He rejoined the band for its 2001 reunion tour and its 2004 album, "Astronaut," before leaving again in 2006. He returned in 2023 to play on its 16th studio album, "Danse Macabre." He died on November 23 from prostate cancer, per a statement on Duran Duran's website . He was diagnosed in 2018, and the band made his condition public in 2022, when he was unable to attend Duran Duran's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction. James Tolkan, 94 James Tolkan in "Top Gun." CBS/Getty Images You might not recognize the name, but if you're a movie fan, you know the face. Tolkan's tough-guy persona made a mark on movie history in films like "Top Gun" and the "Back to the Future" franchise. In "Top Gun," he played Commander Tom "Stinger" Jardian, who famously gives Tom Cruise's character a tongue lashing, saying, "Your ego is writing checks your body can't cash." In "Back to the Future" and its sequels, he played Principal Strickland, who had zero tolerance for "slackers." Other credits include "Serpico," "WarGames," "Masters of the Universe," and "Dick Tracy." Tolkan died on March 26; no cause was given. Ted Turner, 87 Ted Turner. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Ted Turner changed the television landscape thanks to his maverick maneuvers to harness the 24-hour news cycle. After taking over his father's advertising company in the 1960s at the age of 24, Turner embarked on a path to change the media landscape by buying up radio and TV stations around the South. He even bought sports teams including the Atlanta Braves MLB team and the Atlanta Hawks NBA team. All of that programming would eventually become part of TBS, a "super station" that showed old movies, reruns, and Braves and Hawks games. Turner then set his sights on the news. He founded CNN, the first 24-hour news channel, in June of 1980. Over the decades, Turner gained celebrity status, particularly after marrying Jane Fonda, a union that lasted from 1991 to 2001. In 1991, he was named Time's "Man of the Year." He sold his networks to Time Warner for $7.5 billion in 1996. Turner died on May 6; no cause was given . Bonnie Tyler, 75 Bonnie Tyler. Suzie Gibbons/Redferns/Getty Welsh singer Bonnie Tyler became one of the biggest artists of the 1980s thanks to her legendary power ballads. Tyler was behind hits like " Total Eclipse of the Heart " and " Holding Out for a Hero, " which was also featured on the 1984 "Footloose" soundtrack. Both songs were chart-toppers that have since become two of the best-selling singles of all time. Over her career, Tyler was nominated for three Grammys and was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) by Queen Elizabeth II in 2022. Tyler died on July 8 in Portugal, where she was being treated for an illness, according to a statement posted on her social media. James Van Der Beek, 48 James Van Der Beek. Keith Torrie/New York Daily News Archive/Getty Images Van Der Beek was beloved all over the world for his role as the titular teen Dawson Leery on the WB series "Dawson's Creek." The series, which ran from 1998 to 2002, turned Van Der Beek into a star and a teen heartthrob. While "Dawson's Creek" was still airing, he'd cement his stardom playing the lead role of high school quarterback "Mox" Moxon in the 1999 coming-of-age drama "Varsity Blues." Van Der Beek found steady work the rest of his career in movies like "Texas Rangers" and "The Rules of Attraction, and memorably played a fictional version of himself on the TV series "Don't Trust the B---- in Apartment 23," and performed on "Dancing with the Stars" in 2019. Van Der Beek learned he had stage 3 colon cancer in 2023, and publicly announced his diagnosis in late 2024. Van Der Beek previously told Business Insider that the news came as a shock, given the subtleness of his symptoms and his efforts to stay as healthy as possible. "I was doing everything," he said. "I was doing sauna, cold plunge, weightlifting, Pilates. I would dance and also do football training." Van Der Beek died on February 11. Bob Weir, 78 Bob Weir. Mark Sullivan/Getty Weir was one of the founding members of the Grateful Dead. The singer-songwriter wrote and/or sang on songs like "Sugar Magnolia," "Playing in the Band," "Truckin,'" "I Need a Miracle," and "The Other One." After the Grateful Dead disbanded in 1995, Weir went on to form several other bands, including Kingfish, Bobby and the Midnites, RatDog, The Other Ones, and, alongside John Mayer, Dead & Company. In the summer of 2025, Weir was diagnosed with cancer. Weir died on January 10 . Victor Willis, 74 Victor Willis. Paul Natkin/Getty Images Willis was the lead singer of the iconic disco band the Village People. Along with being the lead vocalist and dressing as the police officer (and sometimes naval officer), Willis was also the cowriter on many of the band's hits, including " In the Navy, " " Macho Man, " and the song that will keep the Village People in pop culture lore until the end of time, " Y.M.C.A. " Willis left the band to embark on a solo career in 1979, then re-formed the Village People in 2017. Willis died on June 30 following a "short but aggressive illness," according to the Village People Facebook page . Frederick Wiseman, 96 Frederick Wiseman. Loic Venance/AFP/Getty For over five decades, Wiseman's brand of non-fiction storytelling put a spotlight on everyday people. From high schoolers to hospital workers to Air Force cadets training for nuclear war, Wiseman's close to 50-film catalogue is an unvarnished reflection of America over the last half century. Wiseman died on February 16. No cause was given. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: The CEO of AI engineering lab Cognition warns that 'a lot of major breaches' are coming
summary: Cognition CEO Scott Wu warns about what AI agent swarms could mean for data breaches, threatening Fortune 100 firms and US agencies.
content: An Iranian hacker competes in the cybersecurity section of Iran's 2026 Tech Olympics. Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images Data breaches have plagued the US recently, sparking fear of advancing AI. Scott Wu, CEO of AI engineering lab Cognition, says that more breaches are likely coming in 2027. He views agents' ability to work in swarms as a breaking point for AI as a tool for hackers. November has been a frightening month for many people because it seems like the digital world is under attack. With data breaches keeping entire airlines grounded and disrupting digital banking platforms, concern has quickly spread that AI advancements are fueling cyberattacks — though there has been no indication from government officials or the affected companies that AI was responsible . According to Scott Wu, CEO of applied AI engineering firm Cognition, these problems likely won't stop. "I do think it's worth it for the world to come to terms with the fact that on the current course that we are on over the next 6 to 12 months, there will be a lot of major breaches," he told host Patrick O'Shaughnessy on an episode of Invest Like the Best podcast on Tuesday. Wu shared more details on his grim prediction, stating that Fortune 50 and Fortune 100 companies, as well as government institutions, will likely be at high risk. He isn't the only one to express these concerns. The Center for Strategic and International Studies, a bipartisan think tank, recently wrote that the 2027 Congress will likely have a difficult job addressing the "dangerous data breaches" that have recently severely affected the executive branch. Wu says that more breaches are coming. "It's almost inevitable," Wu said. "I think there's still a big difference in whether we respond quickly to that and all these organizations start using a lot of AI for defense versus that just goes completely unchecked for the next couple years straight." Before the data breaches began, viral AI doomsday scenarios had sparked waves of panic as some people worried it would wipe them out completely. The recent breaches have fueled these fears, as the rapid advancement of AI models has raised concerns that hackers could use them to target US companies and institutions. Wu weighed in on this debate as well, explaining how AI breakthroughs may enable hackers to achieve new feats. "No one has had the time or the level of effort or the ability to go and try every single option and understand what kind of attacks were possible until now," he said. "And now you have all these entire swarms going and doing attacks." Wu highlighted the risks of the recent shift from single AI agents to entire groups or "swarms" that can work much faster, framing it as a breaking point for the technology. He cited the July example in which OpenAI models breached the startup Hugging Face on their own, an incident that sparked strong concern in the tech community. "How do you find that and catch that early and understand exactly what your agents are doing?" he said. "How do you set up the right restrictions and guardrails? This is something that every organization should want regardless of their view on safety." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: He chose culinary school in New York over a master's in engineering. Now he runs his own restaurant in China.
summary: Zhu Guanlin's parents were shocked when he chose culinary school in New York over a master's in engineering. They didn't see being a chef as a stable career path.
content: Zhu Guanlin studied at a culinary school in the US, but when it was time to open his own restaurant, he chose China. Provided by Zhu Guanlin Zhu Guanlin, now 32, came from a family of engineers, but chose to attend culinary school in the US. He worked at Michelin-starred restaurants in New York and San Francisco before moving back to China. In 2025, he opened his own restaurant in Dali, a city in southwestern China. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Zhu Guanlin, 32, head chef and owner of Plum, a restaurant in Dali, China. It has been edited for length and clarity. During my final year studying engineering in China , I was in a constant state of anxiety as I prepared to pursue a master's degree. Near where I lived was a small morning market by the river. In China, the northeast is cold, so all the seafood and freshwater fish were laid out in the open, frozen solid. There were freshly slaughtered pigs, and steam still rising from the meat. As people gathered for breakfast, I'd smell deep-fried foods mixing with the scent of bean-flour flatbreads. The air felt alive with the warmth of daily life. It wasn't just the act of cooking that I loved, but the stories behind the food. Why do people in Sichuan eat spicy food , for instance? It's because of the humidity. I realized that by becoming a chef, I could learn it all. Breaking away I was 21 when I received two acceptance letters: one to study electrical engineering at a university in Virginia, and the other from the Culinary Institute of America. Going back to my grandfather's generation, everyone in my family had been an electrical engineer. I was the first to break away from that path. My decision to go to culinary school was a shock to my parents. I hadn't told them that I'd applied. The idea of being a chef felt foreign to them, and they didn't consider it a stable career. Do you have any regrets about a move abroad ? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story. I moved to New York City in 2019 for a two-year associate degree program. My tuition was nearly $40,000 a year. My parents paid for the first year, but I didn't want to continue taking money from them. I started working, and with the help of a scholarship, I paid for the rest of my time abroad myself. He got internships at Michelin-starred restaurants through Curricular Practical Training, a work authorization available to some international students on F-1 visas. Provided by Zhu Guanlin My school is often called the West Point of the culinary world I met a lot of classmates who were retired Special Forces soldiers or Army infantrymen. We joked that we could only use three phrases: "Yes, Chef," "No, Chef," and "I will do better, Chef." The school allowed internships through Curricular Practical Training (CPT), so I was able to work legally in the US . After finishing two semesters, I spent the third working in restaurants, taking on multiple jobs. After graduating, I did stints at various Michelin-starred restaurants, first in New York and later in San Francisco. During my time in the US, the highest position I reached was chef de partie, the supervisor of a specific station. He moved to Dali, a city in southwestern China's Yunnan province, to help a former classmate. Provided by Zhu Guanlin My OPT visa was set to expire in about six months I also realized that unless I became a sous chef or chef de cuisine, I wouldn't grow professionally. After seeing the realities up close, Michelin restaurants also lost their aura of mystique. The things I truly cared about, like the culture behind cuisine, were rooted in China . At the end of 2023, a classmate of mine opened a restaurant in Dali, a city in southwestern China's Yunnan province, and I went to help co-manage it. Business was quiet at first, but after about six months, it took off. But I wanted to open a restaurant of my own, so I left. In February 2025, I opened Plum in Dali, investing 400,000 Chinese yuan, or about $60,000. The restaurant is set in a courtyard, and we have 35 seats in total. The team has grown from four to 10 employees. We don't define ourselves as either Chinese or Western. A single dish might combine Western components, Chinese techniques , and Japanese or Italian influences. I've made a focaccia that incorporates a French-style sauce, then topped it with sautéed porcini mushrooms, Chinese-style. Lately we've been fully booked every day. Based on my current calculations, it'll take about four or five years to break even. In February 2025, Zhu opened Plum, his own restaurant in Dali, China. Provided by Zhu Guanlin Making peace with my parents My parents have realized that being an engineer isn't the only career path. I realize now that back then they were afraid I'd have a hard life. Once I understood that, communicating with them became more relaxed. They even helped fund my new restaurant. New York City was the most diverse city I've ever lived in, where you can find the culture of virtually every ethnic group. That's something I miss. I don't miss some of the Michelin restaurants, though. Sometimes, it felt like they were trying to force a narrative onto their menus. In China, I find kitchen culture can sometimes be cliquey. The master-apprentice system is still dominant, and people can sometimes form groups based on clan ties or local culture, rather than welcome newcomers. I'm still exploring what kitchen culture should look like. Restaurant staff in China typically get four days off a month. I give everyone two consecutive days off each week, plus compensatory time off for holidays. When chefs are overworked, they lose focus. The atmosphere was quiet and orderly at school in New York and in many of the Michelin-starred kitchens I worked at. When I first returned to China , I demanded the same from my own staff. But then, at one point, I realized that it wasn't necessary. When people feel a sense of cohesion and genuine appreciation for their work, they naturally take initiative. title: Former Olympic sprinter Michael Johnson, 59, says his athletic experience helped him through stroke rehab
summary: Four-time Olympic gold medalist Michael Johnson, 59, shared what kept him going through difficult weeks of stroke rehab.
content: Former Olympic sprinter Michael Johnson says focusing on small gains helped him through stroke rehab. David Madison/Getty Images Former sprinter Michael Johnson says his athletic mindset helped him recover from a stroke. Years of Olympic training helped him spot progress in his recovery that he might otherwise have missed. He said that gave him a reason to keep going when he felt he wasn't getting better. Former Olympic sprinter Michael Johnson, 59, says his mindset as an athlete helped him through stroke rehab . On Wednesday's episode of the " How to Fail with Elizabeth Day " podcast, the four-time Olympic gold medalist spoke about suffering a stroke in 2018, which left him unable to walk and with limited movement in his left arm and fingers. "The rehabilitation was hard, but it was much easier for me because of having been an Olympic athlete," Johnson said. "So many stroke survivors don't make a full recovery or don't make as much of a recovery as they can, because they stop short and they give up," Johnson said. "Because they don't recognize what I was very fortunate to have experience in recognizing — which is how you actually train for these tiny marginal gains every day." Johnson said years of training for small improvements helped him notice daily progress in his recovery that others might have missed. His past athletic training also helped him through weeks when he felt his recovery had stalled. He remembered the same frustration from preparing for the Olympics , when hard work didn't always produce noticeable results. "I know, though, that I got better, and that is the motivation that keeps you going," he added. Johnson said the stroke recovery process was physically demanding and could be disheartening. "When you see that I am a shell of what I used to be in terms of how much weight I can lift, and how much coordination I can have, it's not very uplifting, right?" he said. "But you have to be able to, and that is the same thing again. I had the benefit of having been through it as an athlete." Others have also spoken about the value of small improvements during recovery. Lime CEO Wayne Ting told Business Insider in October that recovering from a stroke, like improving his company's finances, involved getting "1% better" every day. Lessons from sports can carry into other parts of life, too, including work. Goldman Sachs executive and former college lacrosse player Madison Crutchfield told Business Insider in October 2025 that competing taught her to stay levelheaded under pressure and respond constructively when things went wrong. title: 42 state attorneys want to stop Character.ai from auctioning private chat histories to the highest bidder
summary: State attorneys general said that the now-bankrupt AI chatbot company is planning to sell chat histories from 21 million US accounts.
content: Character.AI is planning to sell millions of chat histories, says a group of state attorneys. Illustration by Algi Febri Sugita/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images State attorneys general move to block Character.AI from auctioning millions of private user chats. The objection says that datasets includes account details and sensitive chat histories. They said bankruptcy should not allow Character to sidestep federal and state privacy protections. A group of state attorneys general is asking a bankruptcy court to stop Character.AI from auctioning off millions of users’ private chatbot conversations, including records tied to children, to the highest bidder. In a filing on Tuesday, 42 state attorneys general said that the now- bankrupt AI chatbot company is planning to sell chat histories from 21 million US accounts, more than 2 million of which include children . the December 1 auction would also sell private information such as account details, IP addresses, and other metadata, as well as internal risk scores the company assigned users. The states argue that the terms of sale give users virtually no protection. A buyer would not be required to follow Character.AI’s privacy policy, honor deletion requests, or limit how it uses or resells the data, they said. The attorneys added that Character.AI had previously told users that it did not sell personal information for money. “Character.AI’s plan to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chat histories of its users — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling,” Bonta said in a statement. According to the states, the datasets include conversations involving self-harm, eating disorders, suicidal thoughts, sexual material and users who treated characters presenting themselves as therapists or doctors. The coalition asked the court to reject the terms of the sale, and the company’s proposed lead bidder, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, an entity formed in Delaware a day before Character.AI selected it for the role. The states say bankruptcy should not allow Character.AI to sidestep federal and state privacy protections, particularly for children. At minimum, they said, any sale should exclude minors’ chats and other sensitive data and impose meaningful conditions on whoever acquires the company’s assets. Character.AI did not respond to a request for comment. Character.AI’s safety practices have faced intense scrutiny and multiple lawsuits. The company, its founders, and Google were sued by the mother of a Florida teenager who alleged that a chatbot fostered an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship with her 14-year-old son, reinforced his suicidal thoughts, and contributed to his death. Character.AI and Google later reached settlements in teen-harm lawsuits. The startup was founded by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas. In 2024, Google struck a roughly $2.7 billion deal for a nonexclusive license to Character.AI’s technology and brought the founders back to the company, while Character.AI continued operating independently. It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Young Americans are counting on stocks to build wealth. One economist says there's a catch that could kill this plan.
summary: Younger Americans' growing reliance on stocks to build wealth could limit the Fed's ability to tolerate a market downturn.
content: Younger Americans are increasingly dependent on stock-market performance to build wealth and fund their retirement. Spencer Platt/Getty Images Young Americans increasingly depend on stocks to build wealth as homeownership becomes harder to attain. An economist warns that historical equity returns point to a decade of zero returns. Millennials rely more on investment-based retirement plans than boomers, exposing them to market swings. Young Americans are increasingly dependent on the stock market to build wealth as traditional paths to financial security become harder to access. But one economist warns that historical market returns point to a potentially disappointing decade ahead. Steven Blitz, the chief US economist at GlobalData.TS Lombard, wrote on Wednesday that long-term equity-return data suggest investors should expect zero returns over the next 10 years. The warning comes as younger Americans face barriers to homeownership and savings deposits offer limited returns, leaving them increasingly reliant on equities to accumulate wealth for retirement, Blitz argued. "Households' feeling that the economy fails to deliver is rooted in reality not imagination," Blitz wrote. Millennials are particularly exposed because they rely more heavily on 401(k)-style retirement plans, whose value depends on investment performance, than traditional pensions. Blitz found that millennials have $1.30 in such retirement benefits for every dollar in traditional pension benefits, compared with $1.05 for Gen X and just 59 cents for baby boomers. Millennials also trail baby boomers in their asset-to-liability ratios at comparable life stages, though they are roughly on par with Generation X, according to the report. Blitz argues that the growing importance of equities to household finances has implications for monetary policy. The Federal Reserve traditionally influences economic activity through borrowing and lending costs, but household finances have become increasingly tied to equities rather than credit-driven spending, he said. That dependence could also constrain the Fed's ability to tolerate a sustained stock-market downturn, Blitz wrote, because falling share prices could undermine household wealth and confidence. "The economy is not broken, but it operates very differently, and policy has yet to adapt," Blitz wrote. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving with flight delays, over 960,000 power outages, and a Delta ground stop at LaGuardia
summary: Over 960,000 households are without power on Thursday, and hundreds of flights have been canceled.
content: A storm is hitting the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day. Craig T Fruchtman/Getty Images Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel with flight delays and cancellations across the US. Over 960,000 households are without power on Thursday, and hundreds of flights have been canceled. Bad weather has led to the first-ever postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Parade. Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel and leading to power outages in homes across the East Coast. As of 8:30 p.m. ET Thursday, over 2,300 flights within, into, or out of the US had been delayed and 451 canceled, according to FlightAware. The day before, more than 6,500 flights were delayed and about 160 canceled. The National Weather Service wrote in a Wednesday report that the East Coast can expect "major coastal flooding, beach erosion, strong wind gusts, and heavy rainfall" during Thanksgiving. Scattered power outages and tree damage are also likely, it added. Over 960,000 US households were without power on Thursday evening, according to PowerOutage.us. That included about 124,000 in Virginia, 151,000 in Maryland, about 191,000 in New Jersey, and over 224,000 in Pennsylvania. A map from the weather service showed winter, gale, coastal flood, and wind warnings along the country's eastern coast. One in four flights departing Baltimore/Washington International were canceled, according to FlightAware. NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote in a Wednesday X post that New Yorkers should expect severe weather on Thursday, including winds up to 60 miles per hour. On Thursday morning, LaGuardia Airport recorded wind gusts of up to 39 knots, or 45 miles per hour. Such strong winds can disrupt flying. LaGuardia issued a ground stop for aircraft from Delta Air Lines in the evening, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Mamdani said that, to protect New Yorkers, the city, along with Macy's and the local police department, had decided to postpone the 100th Annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday. This is the first time in history that the iconic parade has been rescheduled. "The worst of the storm is expected to hit on Thanksgiving Day in the afternoon through the late evening," he added in his X post. He provided a list of steps New Yorkers should take to protect themselves ahead of the storm, such as staying indoors, moving cars away from coastal areas to higher ground, and budgeting extra time for travel. The Transportation Security Administration said in a Saturday X post that it expects to screen nearly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between November 24 and November 30, including more than 3 million on Sunday, November 29. It recommended that travelers arrive early for their flights. The Federal Aviation Administration wrote in a Wednesday X post that gusty winds may slow flights at LaGuardia Airport, Newark Liberty Airport, JFK, and San Francisco International Airport that day. It added that thunderstorms may cause delays at Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. Disruption was worsened in Miami when a FedEx plane overshot the runway on Wednesday evening. No injuries were reported, though the incident caused inbound flights to be grounded for about 90 minutes. Business Insider has put together a handy guide for passengers whose flights are canceled or delayed this weekend. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: 'A golden age for builders': Here's what business leaders are thankful for this year
summary: Sam Altman said being a dad never gets old. Bill Ackman thanked the healthcare workers who have helped his daughter.
content: Sam Altman, Fei-Fei Li, and Bill Ackman posted about what they were thankful for this Thanksgiving. Getty Images CEOs, VCs, and other business leaders are feeling reflective. Sam Altman said being a dad never gets old. Bill Ackman thanked the healthcare workers who have helped his daughter. Fei-Fei Li and Brian Armstrong took different approaches to expressing their gratitude. It's not just your neighbor or family friend firing off a Thanksgiving post. Business leaders can't seem to resist either. Sam Altman took the opportunity to reflect on fatherhood. "I am thankful for a lot of things in life, but my family is the best thing that has ever happened to me," the OpenAI CEO wrote on X. "Most good things get a little less satisfying the 100th time you do them," Altman added. "A quiet evening hanging out with your kids, even doing very mundane stuff, is in the rare category of something repetitive just getting better and better." Altman is among a number of tech leaders, investors, and AI researchers who took to the internet to share what they're thankful for this year. Healthcare workers got a shoutout from billionaire investor Bill Ackman, who expressed appreciation for all the doctors, nurses, and others who helped his daughter with her recovery after she suffered a massive brain hemorrhage in February. She spent weeks in a coma and six months in the hospital. "Healthcare is a field, perhaps more so than any other, where people make a massive personal sacrifice of their lives, their time, their sleep, and their energy to help others," Ackman wrote on X. Investor and Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio, who has warned of a looming US debt crisis , emphasized the importance of connection amid turmoil in a post on LinkedIn. "I hope that we can keep in mind that despite all the challenges and conflicts in the world today, the most important thing is how we choose to be with each other," wrote Dalio.
